title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.
why: Worst-case hardness alone does not explain whether feasible procedures can generate instances that remain difficult on average. Resolving this implication would connect the central decision-class separation to robust limits on exact computation under efficiently generated inputs.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin’s robust average-time theory and the Impagliazzo–Levin completeness extension provide the background for distributional NP with samplable inputs.
Bogdanov–Trevisan establish a polynomial-hierarchy consequence for the specified nonadaptive oracle reductions.
The inspected Wigderson edition states the general implication as Open Problem 4.6.
The revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey retains the open question and specifies strict exact samplers, the ensemble parameter and the positive-moment definition.
Liu–Pass publish both a conditional deterministic-description result and a separate randomized-description connection with a specific worst-case premise.
Liu–Mazor–Pass’s ECCC report studies conditional generators and other consequences of specific gap-description hardness; no general NP implication is claimed.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The original book/survey explicitly pose the implication; inspected January and April 2026 results retain specific description-problem hardness assumptions or different distributional guarantees. The July nondeterministic-description abstract does not claim this general implication. No verified derivation from P != NP alone, or proof of its full negation, was found in bounded primary-source checks. The card remains source_open; the cited proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case intractability only says that no single polynomial-time decider works on every input. It gives no immediate frequency statement about difficult inputs under a feasible sampler. The conclusion therefore quantifies over a language together with a fixed distribution ensemble; a different hard input chosen noncomputably at each length is not an admissible sampler.

The positive-moment definition is robust under polynomial changes in running time and machine representation. Rare long computations can affect the first moment much more strongly than a smaller positive moment. Heuristics that sometimes give a wrong answer have a different success condition from the total exact deciders required here.

Distributional completeness is available for polynomial-time samplable ensembles. It identifies problems whose average tractability would imply average tractability throughout the corresponding distributional NP class. Completeness alone does not establish that this class contains a hard problem under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Likewise, easiness under a particular familiar distribution need not reflect worst-case complexity.

Bogdanov–Trevisan show that certain nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Nonadaptive means that all oracle questions are chosen before their answers are read; the reduction must work for arbitrary oracles satisfying its average-correctness promise. This restriction concerns a proof mechanism, not the truth of the unrestricted implication.

Time-bounded description complexity asks how short a program can be while producing a given string within a prescribed time. Liu–Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case connection for a deterministic description problem under an additional exponential circuit-hardness assumption. Section 5 also gives a connection for randomized description complexity without that derandomization assumption, but still assumes worst-case hardness of that particular promise problem. Neither premise has been obtained from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone in the inspected work.

The Liu–Pass paper uses AvgP for a promise-problem notion based on polynomial-time errorless heuristics, separately chosen for each inverse-polynomial failure threshold. This notation must not silently replace the card’s single exact decider and positive-moment bound. The source review records its specific model and hypotheses rather than inferring the requested general implication from a shared class name.

Liu–Mazor–Pass’s April 2026 results concern specific gap versions of description complexity, additional nonuniform hardness or derandomization assumptions, and conditional pseudorandom generators. Their hidden seed distribution can be inefficient to sample. Such a distribution does not meet the efficient sampling requirement in this question merely by existing.

textbook_notes.summary: Does worst-case NP hardness imply distributional average-case hardness?
textbook_notes.status_note: Presented in the cited 2019 source version. The import does not verify present open status; this dated note does not override a later card review.

sentences: The premise P != NP only states a worst-case separation between efficient decision and verification.
The conclusion asks for one fixed NP language and one strict polynomial-time sampler whose generated inputs defeat every deterministic exact decider under a positive-moment runtime bound.
The ensemble parameter is supplied to the decider, while correctness is required even on inputs outside the sampler’s support.
Known reduction barriers concern restricted proof methods, and recent description-complexity results retain specialized hardness premises or different average-case conventions.
A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the implication from the stated premise alone or of its full negation in the ordinary uniform model.

source_formulation.text: The retained question is Wigderson’s worst-case-to-average-case implication, made precise using Bogdanov–Trevisan’s strict exact sampling and deterministic positive-moment convention. In the August 2019 book edition it is Open Problem 4.6, not the numbering in the earlier 2018 draft. The conclusion is existence of an intractable distributional NP problem; this card does not additionally require a named natural distribution or a completeness reduction.

Read Section 1.1.6 and Chapter 2 Sections 2.1/2.2.1 including strict perfect samplability, the separate ensemble parameter, Definitions 3–4 and the explicit statement that the moment bound may be any polynomial. Downloaded the full Bogdanov–Trevisan FOCS 2003 author PDF and read abstract, introduction/reduction scope and Theorems 1–2. The result concerns nonadaptive black-box oracle reductions that must handle arbitrary average-correct oracles; its polynomial-hierarchy consequence is not a proof that the unrestricted implication is false.

Downloaded the final ITCS 2026 Liu–Pass paper and read Section 1.1 Theorems 1.1–1.4, Section 2.1 definitions, Section 2.3 AvgBPP/AvgP convention and Section 5 Theorem 5.1. The deterministic-description consequence uses exponential circuit hardness. The detailed Theorem 5.1 states a randomized-description worst-case premise and is unconditional as a reduction, not unconditional hardness. The opening Theorem 1.4 and detailed statement use differing MINK/MINrK notation; this review relies on the explicit Section 5 statement and does not reproduce a purported cross-measure equivalence. No full proof certification or equivalence of the source’s errorless-heuristic class to the card’s moment class is asserted.

Checked current ECCC TR26-051 page and downloaded the full April Liu–Mazor–Pass paper. Read abstract, introduction, Section 1.1 Theorems 1.1–1.3 and the Section 1.2 description of conditional PRGs. The result retains specific gap-problem hardness, parameter-dependent derandomization/nonuniform assumptions and a potentially inefficient seed distribution; it does not supply the fixed efficient sampler from P != NP.

Only that primary abstract, not its proof, was checked. Recent bibliographic abstracts about Pessiland characterize average-case assumptions rather than deriving them from the bare premise.
